> [!warning] The ending changes with the word class > adjective /dɪˈlɪbərət/ — ends in a weak schwa > verb /dɪˈlɪbəreɪt/ — ends in a long a, as in late > > Same spelling, same stress position, different final vowel. See -ate ending vowel shift.

Sense 1 is the one you will use at work, and its force is intent: a deliberate choice, a deliberate trade-off, a deliberate lie. Oxford's opposite is unintentional.

Note how senses 1 and 2 pull apart in tone. A deliberate decision = on purpose (neutral). He was very deliberate about it = slow and careful (also neutral, but about manner, not intent). Context decides.

The adverb deliberately /dɪˈlɪbərətli/ (B2) carries both: "She's been deliberately ignoring him" (on purpose) and "He packed slowly and deliberately" (carefully).

> [!warning] Vietnamese trap — cố ý is not neutral > English deliberate is neutral: a deliberate trade-off simply describes intent. Vietnamese cố ý leans towards blame — it is the word used in legal contexts (cố ý gây thương tích). Writing "đây là lựa chọn cố ý" about your own design reads as a confession. > Use có chủ đích or có chủ ý for engineering decisions; keep cố ý for when fault is the point.

Useful at work: "That's deliberate" is a one-word way to tell a reviewer something surprising in your code is intentional, not a bug.

items.notesHtml:
From the literal sense — the amount that can be held in one hand, as in a handful of rice. The figurative sense keeps that size: small, and never precise. Think roughly 3–10; never 50.

> [!warning] It downplays > A handful of frames the number as minor. That is a rhetorical choice, not a neutral one. In an incident report, "only a handful of connections were dropped" tells the reader not to worry — so if the real number matters, give the number. Reviewers notice when a vague quantifier is hiding a figure the writer had.

Grammar: takes a plural noun (a handful of connections), and the verb normally agrees with the plural — a handful of requests were retried.

> [!note] Unrelated sense > a handful on its own, of a person, means difficult to control: "Her children can be a real handful." Nothing to do with counting.

Nearby quantifiers by size: a couple of (2) → a handful of (3–10) → dozens of → scores of → hundreds of.

items.notesHtml:
The tech sense comes straight from Oxford's second sense of the verb: to make somebody unable to move by holding them or pressing them against something — "They pinned him against a wall", "her arms were pinned behind her back".

So pinned = held in place, unable to move. Everything the word does in engineering keeps that meaning:

| Phrase | What is held in place | |---|---| | pin traffic to a region | requests can't be routed elsewhere | | session pinning / sticky sessions | a user always reaches the same instance | | CPU pinning | a thread can't migrate to another core | | version / dependency pinning | the version can't drift | | thread pinning (Java virtual threads) | a virtual thread can't unmount from its carrier |

Note the tone shifts with context. Pinning traffic to a healthy region is good — deliberate control. A virtual thread pinned to its carrier is bad — an unwanted constraint. The word is neutral; whether being stuck is desirable depends on what's stuck.

> [!note] A third sense > pin your hopes on something (C2) = to rely on it completely — "The company is pinning its hopes on the new project." Unrelated to holding things down.

items.notesHtml:
Two words doing separate jobs.

runaway — Oxford's third sense: happening very easily or quickly, and not able to be controlled, as in runaway inflation, a runaway success. The image underneath is sense 2: an animal or vehicle no longer under its owner's control. A runaway horse is not moving fast because someone chose that.

degradation — Oxford's specialist sense: the process of something being damaged or made worse, as in environmental degradation.

Together they name something specific: not just "it got worse", but worse in a feedback loop.

> [!tip] The test > Is there a loop where the symptom feeds the cause? Slow responses → clients retry → more load → slower → more retries. If yes, it's runaway. If it just degrades and settles, it's plain degradation.

That distinction is why the phrase earns its place in a postmortem: it tells the reader the system could not recover on its own, which is a different class of incident and needs a different fix — a circuit breaker or a rate limiter, not a bigger machine.

Related: runaway costs, runaway inflation, runaway AI (the sense in the Huang article). Nearby: cascading failure, thundering herd, death spiral.

The whole force of the word is in the original image: Oxford's first sense is a vehicle or engine stopping suddenly from lack of power. The engine is not broken. It just stopped, and it may start again.

That is exactly the right word for a consumer, job or pipeline that is alive but not advancing — and it is precise in a way the neighbouring words are not:

| Word | State | |---|---| | crashed | dead, will not resume | | hung | stopped, usually will not resume | | stalled | stopped, may resume | | slow | still advancing, just late | | throttled | stopped deliberately, by a limit — see CPU Throttling |

Reaching for stalled in an incident report tells the reader "it is not dead, and it is not merely slow" in one word.

> [!warning] A different sense > stall (on/over something) = to deliberately delay so you gain time — "They are still stalling on the deal", "stalling for time". Same verb, opposite implication: that one is intentional.

The rule for well- compounds: > - Before a noun → hyphen: a well-known engineer, a well-documented API > - After a verb → no hyphen: the engineer is well known, the API is well documented > > Since acquainted with almost always follows be, you will almost always write it without a hyphen.

items.notesHtml: advance and advanced are both adjectives but mean different things: advance booking / advance notice = beforehand; advanced English / an advanced model = high level. Pairs to watch: efficiency/efficient, dependence/dependent, consistency/consistent.

items.vi: Hỏi về việc đã xảy ra thì dùng *did* + động từ nguyên mẫu, không dùng hiện tại đơn.
items.notesHtml: Why do you use Vietnamese? asks about a habit — why always. For one finished action it has to be did. Vietnamese marks this with đã / rồi outside the verb, so English feels like it is missing the marker; the marker is the auxiliary.
items.rule: Asking why something **already happened**: *did* + base verb, not the present simple.

items.vi: Sau giới từ, động từ phải ở dạng -ing.
items.notesHtml: The trap is to, which plays two roles. In look forward to and object to it is a preposition, so -ing follows: looking forward to hearing from you. In want to go it belongs to the infinitive, so the base verb follows.
items.rule: After a preposition a verb takes **-ing** — *by, before, after, for, without, instead of*.
